summary: A guide for authors of documents that add new encryption or authentication algorithms to ESP and AH. It maps out how the IPsec documents relate to one another so that new pieces follow a consistent structure. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 6071.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a map of a big pile of IPsec documents. It shows which ones to read and where a new one should fit in.

questions: what is the ipsec document roadmap
how should new ipsec algorithm documents be organized
what goes in an encryption algorithm document for ipsec
subtitle: A guide to organizing new encryption and authentication algorithm documents for IPsec.

tldr.problem: The IPsec protocol suite requires many separate documents for different algorithms and protocols, but there was no clear structure for how new algorithm documents should fit together.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2411 maps out how IPsec documents relate to each other: an Architecture document at the center, with separate documents for ESP and AH protocols, algorithm documents, key management, and a Domain of Interpretation document that ties values together.
tldr.outcome: This roadmap prevents duplicated information and 'draft explosion' by showing exactly where new algorithm documents belong and what they should contain. It was replaced by RFC 6071.

today: RFC 6071 replaces this document as the guide for organizing IPsec algorithm specifications.

sections.title: Introduction and Purpose
sections.content:
RFC 2411 is an informational document that provides guidelines for developing new documents describing encryption and authentication algorithms for the IPsec (IP Security) protocol. The core IPsec protocols—ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload) and AH (Authentication Header)—need a well-organized way to add new algorithms without creating duplicate information across documents.

The main goal is to concentrate on specific algorithms in dedicated documents while keeping general concepts in the core protocol documents. This approach avoids the 'draft explosion' effect, where too many overlapping documents make the specification unclear and hard to maintain.
sections.plainLanguage: IPsec is a way to make data secret and verify it hasn't been tampered with. This document explains how to add new secret codes in an organized way.

sections.title: IPsec Document Organization
sections.content:
The IPsec specification is divided into seven groups of documents that work together. At the top is the Architecture document, which covers general concepts, security requirements, definitions and mechanisms defining IPsec technology.

Below that are the ESP Protocol document and AH Protocol document, which describe packet formats and general issues for their respective protocols. These documents also specify default values and mandatory-to-implement algorithms.

Two parallel sets of documents describe specific algorithms: the Encryption Algorithm documents (for ESP) and the Authentication Algorithm documents (for both ESP and AH). Each algorithm gets its own document describing how to use it within the protocol.

At the center is the Domain of Interpretation (DOI) document, which contains assigned values and constants needed by all the other documents. Below everything are the Key Management documents, describing how keys are negotiated and managed.
sections.plainLanguage: One document explains the overall design, separate documents describe each encryption method, and a central document lists all the numbers and settings that tie them together.

sections.title: Encryption and Authentication Algorithm Documents
sections.content:
Encryption and authentication algorithm documents must cover several required topics. On keying material, they must specify key sizes (minimum, maximum, recommended, required), how to generate strong keys, the format of keying material, any known weak keys, and how often keys should be refreshed.

Each document should include performance considerations: available estimates on the algorithm's performance, comparison data against other algorithms like DES or MD5, and any factors that could improve or degrade performance.

The document must describe payload format and content: the size, placement and content of any algorithm-specific fields not defined in the base ESP or AH documents (such as the initialization vector, or IV).

Each algorithm document must address security considerations: any known attacks, common implementation pitfalls (such as using weak random number generators), and relevant validation procedures and test vectors.
sections.plainLanguage: When you add a new encryption method, the document must explain what size key it needs, how fast it runs, how to store the secret parts, and what can go wrong.

sections.title: Requirements for Encryption Algorithm Documents
sections.content:
Encryption algorithm documents must include a general description of how the algorithm is used in ESP. This includes background material and the formal algorithm description, the features of the algorithm as used by ESP (including encryption and/or authentication), any intellectual property considerations, and references to background material such as FIPS documents.

The document must specify algorithm modes of operation: whether the algorithm operates in block mode or streaming mode, requirements for input or output block format, padding requirements, and any algorithm-specific operating parameters such as the number of rounds.

The specification must identify optional parameters and pick fixed values with explicit technical explanations. For parameters that must remain optional, the document provides defaults and mandatory ranges with explanations of why fixed values would not work.
sections.plainLanguage: The document says how the encryption code actually works inside IPsec and what options are available for making it stronger or faster.

sections.title: Requirements for Authentication Algorithm Documents
sections.content:
Authentication algorithm documents must cover how the algorithm operates with both ESP and AH. Like encryption documents, they must include general information, background material and formal description, features, intellectual property considerations, and references to FIPS documents and definitive descriptions of underlying algorithms.

The specification must describe algorithm-specific operating parameters such as the number of rounds and input or output block format. It must specify padding requirements for the authentication data field (noting that AH has a default padding method). As with encryption documents, optional parameters should be assigned fixed values with technical justifications.

Authentication documents must define the criteria for comparing authentication data, noting that AH has a default verification method. If the algorithm requires a different method (such as verifying a signed hash), the document must explain it.
sections.plainLanguage: When adding an authentication method, the document says how to use it with both encryption and authentication protocols, and how to check that the signature is correct.

sections.title: Key Management and Integration
sections.content:
Both encryption and authentication algorithm documents must specify the key attributes needed by key management protocols: the length of keys, how to pad them, the location of parity bits, the order for multi-keyed algorithms, and the overall key size required.

Key management protocols use the length specifications from algorithm documents to generate keying material of sufficient strength and size. The IPsec Architecture document specifies how keys are extracted from a single block of keying material when multiple keys are required (for example, when using ESP with authentication). Whether the entire keying material passes to the kernel for 'slicing and dicing' or if keys are divided by the key management protocol is an implementation choice for ESP. The AH protocol document has no such requirement.
sections.plainLanguage: The encryption and authentication documents tell the key manager how much secret material to create and how to divide it among different algorithms.
